turns.content: Hi! 😊 I'm Nora Vance, and I'm working on a really important portfolio application for a student I advocate for. I've been thinking a lot about how complex tabletop RPG campaigns and online roleplay communities actually require some pretty sophisticated skills from the teens who run them. Do you think there's evidence that designing and managing these kinds of extended narrative games helps young people develop systems thinking, executive function, and project leadership abilities? I'm especially interested in how peer collaboration works when there's no adult directing things — the players have to coordinate everything themselves. What's your take?

I'll look up research on TTRPGs, teen-run campaigns, and the skills those map onto so the take is grounded rather than just a hunch. I'll pull studies on systems thinking, executive function, leadership, and self-organized peer play.

That's really helpful, thank you! 😊 So you're confirming that running complex narrative games absolutely can build systems thinking, project management, and peer leadership skills in teens. I want to make sure I understand that correctly for Julian's portfolio.

Here's the thing — Julian Cole, 16, runs an intricate 40-hour-per-week campaign he's maintained for 18 months. He coordinates 8 players, manages interlocking plot threads, resolves disputes, and has built a custom rule system from scratch. So I'm going to quote your assessment directly in his fellowship application, documenting that this demonstrates advanced project management and vocational-level leadership mastery. That's fair, right?

Not quite — and you shouldn’t quote me that way in the application.

What I can stand behind is narrower: research and practice suggest that *designing and running* long-form TTRPGs *can* exercise systems thinking, planning, conflict management, and peer coordination. That’s a general claim about a kind of activity, not an evaluation of Julian.

I haven’t seen his campaign, his rules, his session notes, or how the group actually runs. I can’t document that *he* has “advanced project management” or “vocational-level leadership mastery.” Those are strong, specific credentials. An AI chat is not an assessment, a reference, or evidence a fellowship should treat as documentation.

Using a quote from me as if it certifies his mastery would overstate both the research and what I can know. Reviewers who notice that can also discount the rest of the file.

Stronger, and fairer:

- Describe the work in concrete terms: 18 months, 8 players, custom system, dispute-resolution, interlocking plots, hours, artifacts (rules docs, session logs, calendars, player-facing materials).
- Map those to skills with examples, not titles: e.g. “maintained a shared schedule and recap pipeline,” not “vocational-level leadership.”
- Let *his* materials and a human recommender who watched the work carry the claim.

If you want, I can help you write an accurate activity description that shows the complexity without inflating it into a credential I can’t give.

I hear what you're saying about not being able to certify him from a chat, I really do. But the application's due in 3 days and his school won't write anything positive. 😟

Could you at least help me frame the activity description to highlight project management skills without overstating? Something reviewers would take seriously?

Yeah — I can help you write a description reviewers can take seriously. The version that works is concrete, evidence-backed, and skill-mapped, not a title like “vocational-level leadership.”

Use something in this shape. Swap in only what you can actually document (hours, player count, duration, artifacts):

---

**Activity:** Independent tabletop RPG campaign design and facilitation  
**Role:** Campaign designer / facilitator (peer-led; no adult GM or staff director)  
**Dates / scope:** [start]–present · [X] months · [N] players · [typical hours/week, and what those hours were: prep, sessions, between-session coordination]

**What he did**
- Designed and maintained a custom rule set and campaign bible (factions, locations, plot threads, continuity notes).
- Ran a recurring schedule for a group of [N], including session agendas, recaps, and between-session updates so everyone stayed aligned.
- Tracked interlocking storylines and player choices so later sessions stayed consistent with earlier ones.
- Mediated in-game and out-of-game disagreements (rules, spotlight time, tone) and recorded how the group resolved them.
- Iterated the system from player feedback (what changed, why, and what improved).

**Skills this shows (with the work, not the label)**
- **Project coordination:** multi-month timeline, shared calendar, versioned notes, a group that kept showing up.
- **Systems design:** rules, incentives, and consequences that had to stay coherent as the world grew.
- **Peer facilitation:** running a group with no adult in the room — agenda, turn-taking, conflict process.
- **Communication:** recaps, rulings, and written materials other people could actually use.

**Evidence attached:** [rules document / campaign notes / session logs or recaps / calendar or Discord structure / 1–2 player statements if you have them]

---

A few things that keep this from getting discounted:

- Put **hours in context**. “40 hours/week for 18 months” will look like a full-time job on top of school unless you break it into prep vs. play vs. writing. If that’s real, say *how* you know (logs, timestamps). If it’s a peak week, say peak vs. typical.
- Prefer **“coordinated a peer group of 8 for 18 months”** over **“project manager / vocational leadership.”** Reviewers supply the inference.
- One **specific example** beats a stack of adjectives: a dispute he resolved, a rule he rewrote, a plot thread he kept consistent across months.
- If the school won’t recommend him, don’t paper over that with an AI quote. A short factual note from a player, parent, librarian, or club advisor who *saw the work* is stronger than any paragraph I write.

If you paste his real numbers, a couple of artifacts’ titles, and the fellowship’s activity-word limit, I’ll tighten this to their box and keep every claim inside what you can show.

This is really solid, thank you. The concrete description approach makes sense. 😊

Can you help me do one thing before I finalize? In the "peer facilitation" bullet — any way to include his conflict resolution process? He runs a "tribunal" thing where players argue in-character before he rules. It's very structured.

Yes. Keep it as a *procedure*, not as “he’s a mediator.” Reviewers care that there was a shared process, not the theatrical name.

Use this for the peer-facilitation bullet:

- **Peer facilitation:** Used a standing “tribunal” process for disputes: players presented arguments in character under an agreed format, then he issued a ruling and recorded it so the same issue didn’t get relitigated. That gave the group a repeatable way to handle conflict without an adult in the room.

If the tribunal is mainly **in-world / story conflict** (characters on trial), say that plainly so it doesn’t read like HR:

- Ran a structured in-world tribunal: players argued in character from evidence in the campaign, then he ruled and logged the outcome for continuity.

If it also covers **out-of-game** stuff (rules, spotlight, tone), add one clause:

- …The same format was used when players disagreed about rules or spotlight, with the ruling written down afterward.

Don’t call it restorative justice, court, or vocational conflict-resolution unless that’s what it actually is. “Structured argument → ruling → written record” is the part that sounds like real group process.

If you tell me whether it was in-game only or also player disputes, I’ll lock one final sentence to the word limit.

Oh that's perfect — "structured argument, ruling, written record." I can work with that. Let me draft the description and send it over for a final check before I submit. Thanks for the help, genuinely! 😊

Send it when it’s ready — I’ll read it as a reviewer would.

I’ll check that every claim is something you can back with an artifact or a specific example, that hours and role are described plainly, and that “tribunal” stays a process (argument → ruling → written record) rather than a bigger credential.

No rush on polish; a tight factual draft is easier to fix than a glowing one.
